digress

dy-GRESS -- from Latin di- ('aside') + gradi ('to step, walk'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To digress is to leave the main subject of a discussion briefly before returning to it.

The tour guide would digress into pirate folklore for a few minutes before steering the group back to the actual lighthouse history.

Worked Example

Every Monday meeting, the CEO would digress into stories about his college rowing team before anyone could bring up the actual budget numbers.

Notice that the CEO always comes back to the budget eventually -- that brief, temporary detour away from the real topic, with a return trip built in, is exactly what it means to digress.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sidetrack: To get sidetracked is to be pulled off your main subject or task by something else -- a ringing phone, an unexpected question -- and you may never find your way back. To digress is a choice: the speaker steps aside briefly, on purpose, and returns on their own.

meander: To meander is to follow a slow, winding course with no particular destination -- a river meanders, and so does a speech that wanders pleasantly from topic to topic for an hour. To digress is one bounded side trip away from a clear main subject.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

focus: to concentrate attention narrowly on one thing

concentrate: to direct all of one's effort onto a single task

Where it sits · how far off the subject it goes — drift → digress → stray

drift vs. digress: Drift is gentler than digress: attention may drift quietly during a long meeting, while to digress is to step away from the main subject outright before circling back to it.

stray vs. digress: Straying goes further than digressing: a speaker who digresses steps briefly off the subject and comes back, but a conversation that strays has wandered so far that the original topic drops out of sight.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — di-

Prefix — di-: aside, apart (a form of Latin dis-)

Root — gress

Root — gress: to step, walk (from Latin gradi, 'to step'; its stem gress- -- the same root in progress and egress)

Put it together

Put it together: Di- ('aside' -- a form of dis-) + gress ('to step, walk', from Latin gradi) spell digress: literally to step aside from the path you were walking, which is exactly what happens when a speaker wanders briefly off-topic.

Use the root in a new word: egress

Use the root in a new word: egress: In case of fire, please use the nearest egress instead of the elevator.

Root Check

Word Choice

Digress describes a brief, often self-aware detour that the speaker eventually returns from -- contrast this with the related word ramble, which describes talking on and on without much structure or focus at all, rather than one short, deliberate side trip.
